title: LiteLLM supply-chain breach exposes 2,500+ organizations and 434,000 CI/CD pipelines
subtitle: CloudSEK ties the largest AI-infrastructure breach of 2026 to compromised LiteLLM PyPI packages 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 — and to a poisoned Trivy scanner that sat inside the build pipeline for roughly 20 days.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Security researchers at CloudSEK disclosed on August 11, 2026 that a supply-chain compromise tied to the widely used LiteLLM project may have exposed more than 2,500 organizations and roughly 434,000 CI/CD pipelines worldwide — the largest AI-infrastructure breach of the year to date. The named high-confidence exposure list includes NVIDIA, Amazon Web Services, Cisco Systems, Salesforce, Siemens AG, X Corp, and Orange S.A., alongside dozens of finance, telecom, manufacturing, and defense firms.

The attack chain, attributed to a group tracked as Team PCP, began in March 2026 with a compromise of the Trivy security scanner used inside LiteLLM's own build pipeline. That poisoned scanner sat active for roughly twenty days, long enough for the attackers to inject malicious code into LiteLLM PyPI packages 1.82.7 and 1.82.8. Anyone who pulled either version into a build during the window inherited the payload. Potentially exfiltrated material includes AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure credentials; SSH keys; Kubernetes tokens; CI/CD secrets; repository credentials; environment variables; and LLM API keys.

This fits a pattern the AESOP feed has been tracking for months — the AI stack's dependency tree is now the softest attack surface in enterprise infrastructure. LiteLLM is a proxy layer used to route requests to Claude, GPT, Gemini, and dozens of other models from a single interface, which is exactly the kind of high-privilege, high-blast-radius component attackers target. The FBI issued a FLASH advisory in July warning that credentials stolen in earlier LiteLLM-adjacent incidents were still being weaponized; today's disclosure suggests the reservoir of usable stolen secrets is significantly larger than the field previously assumed.

A note for learners: if your organization uses LiteLLM — or any AI-routing proxy that touches production credentials — the immediate action is not to patch, it is to rotate. Every credential that could have transited a compromised build in March needs to be treated as burned, regardless of whether you have direct evidence of misuse. And more broadly, the lesson worth internalizing is that AI infrastructure inherited all of software supply chain's problems the moment it became mission-critical — the mitigations you already know (SBOMs, pinned versions, secret rotation, signed artifacts) are the same ones you need, just applied to a stack that most teams have not yet mapped.
